title: The Broken Oath at Raisen
subtitle: A king famed for justice faces the one decision his own chronicler could not cleanse.
figure: Sher Shah Suri and Puran Mal
era: Siege and massacre at Raisen, 1543 CE
region: Raisen Fort near Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh
moral: History demands truth even when it wounds admiration.

sources.note: Full primary narrative of the Raisen siege, surrender terms, widows' appeal, broken oath and attack.

sources.citation: K.R. Qanungo, Sher Shah and His Times (1965); Satish Chandra, Medieval India, Part II (2007)
sources.note: Modern historians explicitly treat Raisen as a violation of surrender terms.

sources.citation: Ramya Sreenivasan, The Many Lives of a Rajput Queen (2007)
sources.note: Context for Rajput memory, surrender conventions and heroic past-making.

panels.shot: wide, split-composition: Sher Shah on one rampart, Puran Mal on another, Raisen fort between them under stormy skies

dialogue.text: In 1543 at Raisen, Sher Shah Suri swore safe passage to Puran Mal—and his own admiring chronicler then recorded how that oath ended in massacre.

panels.shot: slow push-in on Sher Shah in his command tent, maps and farman scrolls around him

dialogue.text: By 1543, Sher Shah Suri was famed for straight roads, fair revenue, and swift justice. Yet his armies still moved, and Raisen lay outside his order.

panels.shot: medium on Puran Mal atop Raisen’s stone battlements, overlooking rugged countryside

dialogue.text: Raisen’s lord, Puran Mal, held a hill-fort near Bhopal. For Sher Shah, it was a Rajput stronghold he could not ignore on the road that bound his empire.

panels.shot: epic bird’s-eye of the Sur camp ringed around Raisen, siege lines snaking

dialogue.text: Abbas Khan Sarwani, Sher Shah’s own chronicler, tells how the Sur army encircled Raisen. Cannons were placed, trenches dug, the fort shut off from the world.

panels.shot: low-angle from inside Raisen, defenders and families huddled in courtyards

dialogue.text: Days of siege weighed on Raisen. Food shrank, fear grew. Puran Mal’s garrison stood with their families behind heavy gates, knowing Sher Shah’s reputation—and his power.

panels.shot: close three-quarter view of Sher Shah on a rampart of his camp, gesturing toward the fort

dialogue.text: Sarwani writes that Sher Shah preferred terms to needless slaughter. From the siege lines, envoys rode with offers, hoping Raisen would bend without breaking.

panels.shot: tight interior scene, Puran Mal in council with his nobles, lamp-lit faces

dialogue.text: “If the Sur king swears on God, can we trust his word?”

panels.shot: medium on Sher Shah and envoys facing each other in open field, hands raised solemnly

dialogue.text: According to Sarwani, Sher Shah swore a solemn promise: safe passage for Puran Mal, his family, and retinue if they surrendered Raisen and left his territory.

panels.shot: dramatic close-up on Puran Mal’s face as he looks from fort walls toward the Sur camp

dialogue.text: The chronicler says Puran Mal accepted. Raisen’s gates would open. In return, the Rajput lord staked everything on the Sur king’s sworn word.

panels.shot: wide moving column shot: Puran Mal’s people leaving the fort, carts, horses, slow procession

dialogue.text: Sarwani describes them leaving the fort under truce, guarded by Sur troops. It was the fragile, dangerous moment when surrender relied only on trust.

panels.shot: interior camp scene, close on a group of Muslim survivors pleading before Sher Shah

dialogue.text: Then Sarwani’s story turns. Muslim survivors from Chanderi came before Sher Shah, accusing Puran Mal of having earlier enslaved and abused them.

panels.shot: tight, conflicted close-up on Sher Shah’s face, shadow cutting across

dialogue.text: Sarwani reports their words stirred Sher Shah’s fury. Justice for the oppressed stood against the oath just sworn. In that tension, the king had to choose.

panels.shot: medium shot of Sher Shah issuing orders to Isa Khan Niazi, finger pointing toward the departing column

dialogue.text: Sarwani says Sher Shah ordered Isa Khan Niazi to pursue Puran Mal’s column and destroy it. The safe-conduct was set aside; the oath was broken.

panels.shot: tense long shot: Isa Khan’s cavalry bearing down on the marching column at a distance

dialogue.text: No body counts are given. But Sarwani is clear: Isa Khan’s men overtook them, and the garrison and families who had trusted the oath were destroyed.

panels.shot: somber mid-shot: Puran Mal in the midst of chaos, turning decisively toward his kin

dialogue.text: Rajput memory, as studied by modern historians, would later shape this moment into heroic last stands and tragic choices. But the core fact remains: the surrendered column was attacked.

panels.shot: wide aftermath shot: empty field with abandoned belongings, Raisen fort looming far behind

dialogue.text: K.R. Qanungo and Satish Chandra read Sarwani’s account plainly: Sher Shah violated terms he had sworn. Raisen became the dark exception to his fame for justice.

panels.shot: reflective mid-shot: Sher Shah alone on a ridge at dusk, looking toward Raisen

dialogue.text: Sarwani, loyal to Sher Shah, still records the broken promise and massacre. He does not excuse it; he preserves it as part of the king’s real reign.

panels.shot: conceptual split shot: one half showing Sher Shah’s road and sarai, other half Raisen’s desolate hill

dialogue.text: Thus Sher Shah’s legacy holds both: ordered roads, reformed revenues, and also Raisen—a place where royal justice met anger and broke its own word.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on an unseen narrator’s weathered hand closing a manuscript bearing Sarwani’s name

dialogue.text: Raisen reminds us that history’s truest honor is not in protecting reputations, but in keeping faith with the record—even when it wounds kings we admire.
